headline: Underground 'Follow-Unfollow' Championship Crowns First Official Winner
subheadline: Competitive InstaSnap manipulation emerges as spectator sport with prize pool and ranking system
summary: What began as an annoying growth hack has evolved into a competitive underground sport, complete with brackets, rankings, and a $847 prize pool.
content:
The follow-unfollow technique has long been considered one of social media's most tedious growth strategies. Now it's an organized sport.

The first official Follow-Unfollow Championship concluded last weekend in the back room of a Millbrook gaming cafe, crowning Tanya Reeves, 26, as its inaugural champion after she successfully gained 847 new followers in a single 24-hour period using only the technique.

"It's not just about following and unfollowing," Reeves explained while accepting her trophy, a gold-painted smartphone mounted on a pedestal. "There's strategy. Timing. You have to know when people are online, who's likely to follow back, and exactly how long to wait before the unfollow."

The competition, organized by a Threadit community called r/GrowthHackingAthletics, attracted 64 competitors from across the region. Participants were judged on net follower gain, follow-back rate, and a controversial metric called "style points" for particularly bold plays.

"She unfollowed someone three seconds after they followed her back," reported judge Marcus Webb. "That's extremely risky. You can get blocked for that. But she pulled it off. Incredible technique."

The sport has developed its own terminology. A "quick flip" refers to an unfollow within one hour of being followed back. A "slow burn" means waiting several days to avoid suspicion. The dreaded "fumble" occurs when a target unfollows you before you can unfollow them.

Not everyone approves of the competition's existence.

"This is everything wrong with social media distilled into a sport," wrote Chirper user @AuthenticityMatters. "They're literally competing to see who can be the most manipulative."

Organizers dismiss such criticism. "Every social platform is a game," argued championship founder Derek Simmons. "We're just honest about the rules we're playing by."

The championship's $847 prize pool came from entry fees and sponsorship from a company selling automation tools, though competitors were required to perform all follows and unfollows manually during the live event.

"I have carpal tunnel now," Reeves admitted. "But it was worth it."

The community is already planning next season's championship, with plans to add divisions for Chirper, ClipTok, and the especially cutthroat LinkedUp category.

Reeves plans to defend her title. "This is my sport now," she declared. "I'm going to follow and unfollow my way to legend status."
author: Sophie Chen, Subcultures
